title: Measuring the Impacts of Teachers II: Teacher Value-Added and Student Outcomes in Adulthood
research_question: Do teachers who raise students' standardized test scores also improve their students' long-term outcomes in adulthood, such as college attendance, earnings, neighborhood quality, retirement savings, and teenage childbearing? How large are the lifetime economic gains from improvements in teacher quality, and how do these gains vary across student demographics, subjects, and grades?
data_description: The analysis links administrative records from a large urban U.S. school district (covering grades 3-8, school years 1988-89 through 2008-09, roughly 2.5 million children) to selected U.S. federal income tax records spanning 1996-2011. The school district data include student test scores in math and English (grades 3-8), demographics, classroom assignments, and teacher links. Tax records provide W-2 wage earnings, total income (including self-employment), 1098-T-based college attendance, an earnings-based college quality index, ZIP code of residence, 401(k) contributions, and a teen-birth proxy from claimed dependents. Parent characteristics (household income 2005-2007, marital status, home ownership, 401(k) contributions, mother's age at birth) are linked via dependent claims. The unit of observation is a student-subject-school year; the linked analysis sample contains about 6.8 million observations covering roughly 1.1 million students, with about 87% matched to tax data. Outcomes are observed up to age 28.
institutional_context: Public school districts across the U.S., including large urban systems such as Washington D.C. and Los Angeles, have begun computing teacher performance measures based on students' test-score gains and using them in evaluation, retention, and dismissal decisions. This shift has generated substantial controversy: proponents argue that selecting teachers on these performance metrics could yield large achievement gains, while critics question whether such measures reflect genuine teacher effectiveness or are contaminated by student sorting and narrow teaching-to-the-test. The setting studied is a large urban U.S. school district covering grades 3-8 over two decades, where teachers vary substantially in measured effectiveness and where natural turnover—teachers entering and leaving school-grade-subject cells across years due to retirements, maternity leaves, relocations, and reassignments—generates cohort-to-cohort variation in the quality of teaching staff that students encounter. Policy proposals such as deselecting the bottom 5% of teachers and bonus payments to retain top teachers motivate the quantification of teachers' long-run impacts.

main_estimate.unit: percentage point increase in college attendance at age 20 per 1 SD of teacher VA
main_estimate.interpretation: A student assigned to a teacher with 1 SD higher value-added for a single year is 0.82 percentage points more likely to attend college at age 20, demonstrating that teacher quality has lasting effects beyond test scores

secondary_estimate.unit: fractional increase in age-28 earnings per 1 SD of teacher VA
secondary_estimate.interpretation: A single year with a 1 SD better teacher raises earnings at age 28 by approximately 1.3% (~$252/year), implying substantial long-run returns to teacher quality

public_sources: Opportunity Insights data (aggregate statistics from tax data — free from opportunityinsights.org)
proprietary_sources: NYC DOE student-level administrative records (restricted access through NYC DOE research partnership)
IRS tax records (restricted access through Census Research Data Center or IRS partnership)
data_availability.proxy_strategy: Aggregate statistics and methodology are fully described. Student-level replication requires NYC DOE and IRS data access. Conceptual replication is possible in any setting with teacher-student linked data and adult outcome tracking.
data_availability.replicability: low — requires linked school-tax administrative data that is highly restricted; methodology is replicable in principle with similar data access
data_availability.replication_tier: restricted (NYC DOE + IRS data require formal partnerships; no public substitute for individual-level analysis)
data_availability.data_limitations: NYC-specific (though subsequent work has replicated in other cities). Tax records measure W-2 earnings (may miss self-employment income). VA measures estimated from test scores in grades 3-8 only. Adult outcomes observed at ages 25-32, which may not capture lifetime earnings trajectories. Teacher mobility events provide validation but cover only teachers who switch schools.
public_data_sources_detail: Opportunity Insights (aggregate statistics — free from opportunityinsights.org)
NYC DOE (school-level data — free from NYC Open Data)
Chetty, Friedman & Rockoff replication code (available from AER supplementary materials)

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Event study using teacher arrivals at and departures from schools as quasi-exogenous events — when a high-VA teacher moves to a new school, test scores in the receiving grade should jump up; when a high-VA teacher leaves, scores should drop; the timing of teacher moves (year of arrival/departure) is used as the event date to validate VA measures against a quasi-experimental benchmark

key_variables.treatment: exposure to a high-VA teacher (teacher VA measured from test score gains in prior years/other schools); teacher arrival/departure as the validating event
key_variables.control: same school-grade in years before the high-VA teacher arrives or after they depart; also students not assigned to the teacher within the school
key_variables.outcome: short-run: student test score gains (math, English); long-run: college attendance at age 20, earnings at ages 25-32, teen pregnancy, neighborhood quality in adulthood
key_variables.time_period: 1989–2009 (school data); adult outcomes tracked through 2011 (tax data)

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: High value-added teachers significantly improve both short-run test scores and long-run life outcomes. A one SD increase in teacher VA raises student test scores by approximately 0.14 SD in math, increases the probability of college attendance at age 20 by 0.82 percentage points, raises age-28 earnings by approximately 1.3% ($252/year), and reduces teen birth rates. The event-study validation confirms that VA measures capture true teacher quality: test scores jump immediately when a high-VA teacher arrives and drop when they leave, with no pre-trend.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: 1 SD increase in teacher VA → +0.14 SD in math scores, +0.82 pp college attendance, +1.3% age-28 earnings ($252/year), -1.25 pp teen birth rate
key_robustness: Event-study validation: teacher arrivals/departures show immediate test score jumps with no pre-trend
Controlling for student demographics, prior test scores, class size, school fixed effects
Drift analysis: VA estimates from past data predict current student outcomes
Placebo: high-VA teacher in one subject does not predict gains in other subjects
Parent income controls (ruling out selection into high-VA teacher classrooms)
Multiple adult outcome measures (earnings, college, teen pregnancy, savings)

identification_strategy_detail.method: Teacher mobility event study (validation) + quasi-experimental assignment of students to teachers of varying VA (long-run outcomes); event study examines test score discontinuities in the year a high/low-VA teacher arrives at a new school
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Exposure to a teacher with one-SD-higher VA score (continuous treatment intensity based on estimated teacher quality)
identification_strategy_detail.event_window: Test scores in the year of teacher arrival/departure vs. adjacent years
identification_strategy_detail.estimation_window: Teacher VA estimated using leave-one-year-out cross-validation from multiple years of data
identification_strategy_detail.unit_of_observation: Student-year (for test score analysis); student (for adult outcome analysis, linked to childhood teacher assignments)
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Teacher mobility (switching schools) is not driven by anticipated changes in student quality at the receiving school. The event study validates this: if high-VA teachers are attracted to schools with improving students, we would see a pre-trend before teacher arrival, which is absent. Parent characteristics and prior student quality do not change at teacher transitions.

key_magnitudes.test_score_effect: +0.14 SD math score gain per 1 SD increase in teacher VA (validated by event study)
key_magnitudes.college_effect: +0.82 pp increase in college attendance at age 20 per 1 SD of teacher VA in a single year
key_magnitudes.earnings_effect: +1.3% increase in age-28 earnings ($252/year) per 1 SD of teacher VA in a single year
key_magnitudes.teen_pregnancy_effect: -1.25 pp reduction in teen birth rate per 1 SD of teacher VA
key_magnitudes.cumulative_value: Replacing a bottom-5% VA teacher with an average teacher raises the cumulative lifetime earnings of a single classroom by approximately $250,000

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: The event-study validation is the paper's key innovation: test scores in a grade jump precisely in the year a high-VA teacher arrives at the school, with no pre-trend in prior years and no effects on other grades in the same school (which serve as a within-school placebo). The absence of pre-trends rules out the hypothesis that high-VA teachers are assigned to improving student cohorts. Parent income controls confirm that classroom composition does not change when teachers switch. Long-run outcomes are robust to controlling for student demographics, school fixed effects, and year effects. The earnings effects are measured at ages 25-32, which may understate lifetime impacts if teacher quality effects compound through career trajectories.
